UMA-Aware Execution Layer Figure 5 . Asymmetric weight layouts in EdgeAgent for zero-copy heterogeneous TP on the Apple M4 SoC. CPU shards are pre-packed into 16×64 FP16 tiles to maximize SME utilization, while GPU shards retain a linear SIMT layout. 3.1.1. Zero-Copy TP We design a UMA-aware heterogeneous computation graph that maximizes TP performance on edge devices through two key structural optimizations. First, to bridge the micro-architectural gap between processors, the graph enforces an asymmetric weight layout (Figure 5 ). GPU shards retain a standard linear layout for SIMT, while CPU shards are offline pre-packed into 2D tiles for SME, satisfying the memory stride constraints of both units. Second, to eliminate memory copy overhead, we allow both devices to concurrently write their partial output results directly into a single shared physical buffer. Model partitioning and weight residency. EdgeAgent partitions each transformer block with two patterns, both fixed at load time. (1) Every linear projection, including the MLP gate/up/down projections and the attention Q/K/V/O projections, is column-parallel along the output (N) dimension. A weight matrix W ∈ ℝ K × N W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times N} is split along its N (output-column) dimension into W c ​ p ​ u ∈ ℝ K × n W_{cpu}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times n} and W g ​ p ​ u ∈ ℝ K × ( N − n ) W_{gpu}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times(N-n)} , where n = α ⋅ N n=\alpha\cdot N and each layer’s split ratio α \alpha is computed from its K/N dimensions to equalize CPU and GPU compute time. Both devices read the same activation from shared memory and write disjoint column ranges of one preallocated output buffer, so no cross-device reduction is ever needed. (2) The attention core is partitioned by heads: the GPU runs a fused SDPA over its head range while the CPU runs a grouped matmul over the remaining heads, with the per-head score/softmax/context computation entirely device-local. The two head-group contexts are then recombined by a single concat along the head axis before the column-parallel O projection. Weights are stored once: GPU shards keep their native SIMT layout, and only CPU shards are repacked offline at initialization into the SME 16 × 64 16\times 64 tile layout, after which the temporary unpacked CPU copies are freed; EdgeAgent therefore holds exactly one copy of the model weights (Figure 5 ). However, realizing this zero-copy, in-place mutation fundamentally conflicts with the functional semantics of modern lazy computation graphs. In standard ML compilers, graph abstractions inherently conflate logical data dependence with physical memory materialization. Merging CPU and GPU sub-tensors strictly requires a concat operator, which is lowered into explicit memory allocations and copy kernels, thereby wasting the hardware benefits of UMA. Conversely, performing a naive in-place write into a shared buffer violates the DAG’s tensor-level dependency tracking. Without explicit data-flow edges, the instruction scheduler cannot guarantee execution order, leading to severe data hazards (e.g., downstream operators reading stale data) unless penalized by conservative, eager synchronization. To safely merge CPU and GPU results without triggering memory copies or breaking data dependencies, we modify the graph execution via two lightweight mechanisms: (1) Logical Dependency Barrier: We replace the standard concat operator with a custom barrier node. Logically, it acts as a synchronization point in the DAG, ensuring downstream operators wait for both processors to finish. Physically, it allocates zero memory, simply aliasing the output pointer to the underlying shared buffer. (2) Heterogeneous Fast Path: As the logical barrier handles the graph dependencies, we can execute this specific subgraph outside the framework’s generic scheduling loop. This dedicated fast path issues concurrent tasks directly to the CPU and GPU without inserting conservative cross-device hardware fences, achieving a truly lock-free, zero-copy concurrent execution. Coherence and memory-model assumptions. EdgeAgent does not introduce a new coherence protocol. It relies on the coherence already provided by the UMA SoC: the CPU and GPU share a single physical address space and are kept coherent through the system-level cache, so a write issued by either device to a shared buffer is visible to both devices without explicit cache flushes or host–device copies. This single coherence domain is exactly the property that the concat-based path in stock MLX discards, since concat materializes a new contiguous array and copies both halves into it. Consistency, however, is weak rather than sequential: Metal follows a weak, relaxed memory model, where cross-device visibility is not guaranteed without explicit synchronization. Our Heterogeneous Fast Path therefore establishes only the producer–consumer happens-before relation the design actually needs. The MLP projections and the attention Q/K/V/O projections are all column-parallel, so the CPU and GPU write disjoint column ranges: no address is ever written by both devices, so there is no data race and no fine-grained per-line coherence is required. The Logical Dependency Barrier encodes the remaining ordering as a graph dependency, a zero-copy node that aliases the shared buffer, so MLX’s lazy evaluation orders downstream operators after both producers finish, with no explicit hardware fences or eager synchronization. 3.1.2. SME Micro-kernel Optimization Maximizing the efficiency of the CPU requires saturating the SME units. The system achieves this saturation through a tightly coupled hierarchy of micro-optimizations. At the single-core instruction level, we partition the matrix workloads into 16 × 64 16\times 64 micro-tiles. This specific dimension is purposefully chosen to simultaneously saturate the memory bandwidth using continuous multi-vector loads ( svld1_x4 ) and to keep all four 2D ZA register tiles maximally occupied. By aggressively unrolling loops along the K dimension, the kernel physically overlaps these continuous memory loads with the outer-product accumulation. This software pipelining effectively masks memory access latencies. To ensure these saturated compute pipelines are not abruptly starved by cache thrashing, we systematically tune the macro-tiling parameters. By strictly confining the active memory footprint within the 8MB effective L2 working set, the system avoids sharp bandwidth degradation and maintains continuous data ingestion. However, scaling to full SoC utilization exposes load imbalance. The asymmetric multiprocessing (AMP) topology of modern edge chips, which mixes high-throughput P-cores with slower E-cores, as illustrated in Figure 5 , inevitably induces straggler effects under traditional static task binding. To mitigate these straggler effects, we deploy a lock-free dynamic work-stealing mechanism. Built entirely upon relaxed-consistency atomic operations, this decentralized queue allows heterogeneous worker threads to autonomously steal compute micro-tiles based on their real-time physical execution rates. This achieves optimal fine-grained load balancing across the asymmetric hardware topology without ever incurring lock contention overheads. 3.2. Agent-Aware Scheduling Layer The scheduling layer acts as the bridge between multi-agent workflows and the physical hardware constraints. We first determine the optimal global drafting budget M M from hardware profiling results. As shown in Figure 6 , the SME matrix multiplication kernel exhibits a strict stage performance behavior. Driven by 16 × 64 16\times 64 micro-tiles, the matmul performance scales in discrete jumps at batch size multiples of 16, with efficiency plateauing between these thresholds. Critically, beyond a draft length of 16, the performance degrades sharply, establishing an upper bound for efficient batch processing. Furthermore, Figure 3 also validates this choice through end-to-end speculative decoding profiling. For high-acceptance-rate tasks (Structured Output Task), the maximum speedup of 1.69 × \times is achieved at a draft length of 16, after which performance begins to degrade due to rising rejection overhead. Therefore, to align with the hardware efficiency of both CPU and GPU units, we set the global drafting budget to M = 16 M=16 token slots. Given this fixed hardware-aligned capacity, the scheduling layer employs two dynamic mechanisms to maximize the utility of these slots. 3.2.1. Dynamic Drafting Budget Allocation Figure 6 . The stage performance of SME matmul. To reliably saturate these 16 hardware slots without forcing a single request to over-expand its speculative tree (which suffers from diminishing returns in acceptance yield), the system pools multiple concurrent agents into a unified physical batch. However, uniformly dividing this fixed 16-token budget fails to account for the extreme variance in the difficulty of drafting across streams. Static allocation strategies inherently bottleneck parallel efficiency by over-provisioning execution slots to difficult tasks while under-resourcing highly productive ones. To dynamically allocate draft length based on these runtime characteristics, we propose an agent-aware scheduler . By introducing the Historical Accepted Length (HAL) as an objective proxy for the underlying drafting difficulty, this scheduler seamlessly captures the real-time generation state of each concurrent stream. The HAL tracks the absolute number of accepted tokens rather than the acceptance rate. Relying on percentages obscures an agent’s true throughput contribution, as a shallow draft tree might exhibit a perfect acceptance rate while yielding minimal tokens. HAL is therefore a lightweight heuristic rather than a globally optimal metric: it steers the fixed L t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l = 16 L_{total}=16 slots toward agents that yield more accepted tokens per verification step. After the t t -th verification step, the scheduler applies an exponential moving average (EMA) to update the HAL for each active agent i i : A i ​ ( t ) = γ ⋅ k i ​ ( t ) + ( 1 − γ ) ⋅ A i ​ ( t − 1 ) A_{i}(t)=\gamma\cdot k_{i}(t)+(1-\gamma)\cdot A_{i}(t-1) where k i ​ ( t ) k_{i}(t) represents the absolute count of accepted tokens in the current step. The decay factor γ \gamma dictates the responsiveness to sudden shifts in drafting difficulty within the generative stream. In practice, we perform an exhaustive grid search over candidate hyperparameters using profiling data from heterogeneous multi-agent workloads. The decay factor γ = 0.3 \gamma=0.3 and initial prior of A i ​ ( 0 ) = 4.0 A_{i}(0)=4.0 are selected as the optimal combination that maximizes end-to-end system throughput, effectively balancing responsiveness to workload variations and noise robustness. For the subsequent decoding step t + 1 t+1 , the scheduler must partition the global drafting budget L t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l = 16 L_{total}=16 across N N concurrent agents. To structurally guarantee starvation-free forward progress, the system provisions a non-preemptible baseline capacity, L m ​ i ​ n L_{min} , for each agent. The residual budget is then dynamically allocated using a temperature-scaled softmax distribution over the agents’ HAL: L i ​ ( t + 1 ) = L m ​ i ​ n + ⌊ ( L t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l − N ⋅ L m ​ i ​ n ) ⋅ exp ⁡ ( A i ​ ( t ) / τ ) ∑ j = 1 N exp ⁡ ( A j ​ ( t ) / τ ) ⌋ L_{i}(t+1)=L_{min}+\left\lfloor(L_{total}-N\cdot L_{min})\cdot\frac{\exp(A_{i}(t)/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(A_{j}(t)/\tau)}\right\rfloor This agent-aware control loop autonomously skews the draft length allocation toward high-yield agents. Consequently, it physically truncates the speculative draft trees of difficult-to-draft workloads, strictly bounding non-productive compute exploration and memory overheads based purely on empirical acceptance signals. Allocation is bounded on both sides by this formula. Because every agent reserves the non-preemptible L m ​ i ​ n L_{min} first, the softmax only distributes the residual L t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l − N ∗ L m ​ i ​ n L_{total}-N*L_{min} , so even the highest-HAL agent cannot capture the full L t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l = 16 L_{total}=16 budget. Because HAL is recomputed through the EMA at every verification step, a transient burst cannot permanently lock out other agents. 3.2.2. Cooperative Suspend-and-Yield Mechanism External tool invocations inevitably stall individual execution streams. In a strictly hardware-aligned concurrent batch, a stalled agent occupying active token slots will directly degrade global throughput. To explicitly neutralize these latencies, the agent-aware scheduling layer implements an OS-inspired cooperative suspend-and-yield mechanism tied directly to the speculative budgeting system. At the synchronization boundary of each verification step, the scheduler inspects agent execution states. Upon detecting a tool-induced stall, it triggers a cooperative yield, migrating the stalled agent to a suspended queue and instantly relinquishing its allocated token slots back to the global drafting budget. Relinquishing these slots allows the dynamic allocator (Section 3.2.1 ) to instantly redistribute the yielded budget across the remaining active agents. By absorbing the vacated budget, active streams dynamically expand their draft trees, broadening their speculative search space without breaking the optimal hardware-aligned 16-token threshold. Crucially, by exploiting the physically shared addressing of the UMA architecture, the system performs an in-place metadata freeze on the suspended agent’s KV cache. Upon resolution of the external tool execution, the scheduler promotes the ready agent back to the active queue to request fresh token slots. As the underlying memory pool guarantees in-place KV freezing and hardware-aware offset-remapping compaction, the awakened agent directly resumes speculative execution. This tightly integrated memory management explicitly eliminates the need for expensive context re-prefill phases, achieving strictly zero-overhead state restoration. 4. Evaluation EdgeAgent builds upon Apple’s native MLX runtime, fundamentally restructuring its underlying C++ graph executor to enable zero-copy UMA memory management. Furthermore, it introduces lightweight cross-layer APIs to synchronize multi-agent execution states such as variance in drafting difficulty and tool-induced stalls with the underlying scheduler. We comprehensively evaluate EdgeAgent using trace-driven multi-agent workflows to demonstrate its end-to-end makespan, concurrent throughput, and resilience to tool-induced execution stalls. 4.1. Experimental Setup Hardware Testbed. Primary experiments are conducted on an Apple M4 SoC equipped with 32 GB of unified memory and a 120 GB/s UMA bus. The SoC integrates a 10-core CPU (4 performance + 6 efficiency) with the ARMv9 SME2 extension, alongside a 10-core GPU. To verify EdgeAgent ’s generalization, the key ablations are additionally evaluated on an Apple M4 Pro SoC with 64 GB of unified memory and a 273 GB/s UMA bus, whose 14-core CPU (10 performance + 4 efficiency) and 20-core GPU shift the compute-to-bandwidth balance relative to the base M4.
